spoken: Press a key on this machine, and a lamp lights up another letter.
Press the same key again, and a different lamp lights, and then another.
In the war, the army's version could be set up in nearly a hundred and fifty-nine quintillion ways.
A hundred and fifty-nine quintillion? That sounds unbreakable.
But it had one odd habit. It never turned a letter into itself.
That small rule, and the people who saw what it meant, helped break Enigma.
Enigma has twenty-six keys and twenty-six lamps. One operator types; another writes down the lamps that light.
So let's follow one key press. First, the key turns the right-hand rotor one step.
Then the current runs to the plugboard, where a cable can swap it for another letter.
And here, A is plugged to Q.
Next come three rotors, each wired inside to turn one letter into another.
At the far end, the reflector sends the current back another way.
Back through the plugboard, and one lamp lights. Here, the letter A became C.
Now press A again. The rotor has moved, so every wire has shifted. A becomes N.
So the same key gives a new letter, because every press uses a fresh scrambled alphabet.
Do the other two rotors ever move?
Once per turn, a notch lets the right rotor push the middle one along, like a car's odometer.
Almost. The middle rotor sometimes steps twice in a row, which is called the double step.
So it's not quite an odometer.
No. The rotors come back to where they started only after sixteen thousand nine hundred key presses.
The reflector joins the 26 letters in 13 pairs, and turns the current round.
So the machine works both ways. At the same setting, press the letter C, and the current runs backwards to A.
Set a second machine the same way, type in the ciphertext, and out comes the message.
There's no switch between coding and decoding at all.
But there's a catch. Could a key ever light its own lamp?
Only if the current came back along the very wire it went in on.
That would mean the reflector joining a letter to itself, and it never does.
So no letter is ever enciphered as itself. Press A, and you get anything but A.
We tried every key at every rotor position. Not one lit its own lamp.
Couldn't the plugboard fix that?
No. It swaps a letter on the way in, and swaps it back on the way out.
So how many ways could the army's Enigma actually be set up?
Let's count. There are three rotors from a box of five, and ten plugboard cables.
Choosing the rotors and their order gives 5 times 4 times 3, which is 60 ways.
Their starting positions give twenty-six times twenty-six times twenty-six, which is seventeen thousand five hundred and seventy-six.
And ten cables pairing up letters on the plugboard give about a hundred and fifty-one trillion ways.
Multiply them, and that's nearly 159 quintillion settings, even before the rotors' ring settings.
At a million settings a second, trying them all would take about five million years.
No wonder its users felt safe.
But nobody broke Enigma by trying every setting. They found shortcuts, and the first came from Poland.
In nineteen twenty-nine, Poland's Cipher Bureau trained German-speaking mathematics students in Poznan, in secret.
Why did they want German speakers?
Poznan had been German before the First World War.
In September 1932, the Bureau took on three of them, Marian Rayefski, Yerzy Roozhitski, and Henrik Zigalski.
Rayefski spotted a German habit. Each message began with its own rotor setting, typed twice, from a start shared that day.
So the first and fourth letters hide the same letter. So do the second and fifth, and the third and sixth.
From a day's messages, those links join up into loops, which come in pairs of the same length.
And the plugboard changes which letters sit in each loop, but never how long the loops are.
So the lengths of the loops point to the rotor settings, whatever the plugboard does.
A cryptology scholar later called this the theorem that won World War Two.
Rayefski still needed the rotors' wiring. Help came from a spy.
Hans-Thilo Schmidt, at Germany's Cipher Office, sold secrets to the French, including two months of keys from nineteen thirty-two.
And in December, the French shared them with Poland.
Another puzzle was the keys' wiring. Rayefski guessed plain order, A to A and B to B, and he was right.
So it was just the alphabet, in order.
By the end of nineteen thirty-two, he had all three rotors and the reflector, without ever seeing the machine.
From January nineteen thirty-three, the Poles read Enigma. As the Germans tightened their rules, they kept finding new ways in.
From September 1938, each operator picked his own start, but still typed the key twice.
Sometimes a repeated letter came out the same twice. Zigalski punched sheets with holes wherever that could happen.
Stack the sheets for a day's messages, line them up, and fewer and fewer holes shine through.
Here are seven, from a simulated day. The one hole left gives away the ring settings.
And they cut all those holes by hand?
Yes, they cut them by hand, with razor blades.
Rayefski also designed the bomba, which was in effect six Enigmas wired together and driven by a motor.
Six were built, one for each order of the rotors. A day's key took about two hours.
Then, in December nineteen thirty-eight, the Germans added two more rotors. Three from five made sixty orders, not six.
Sixty bombas would have cost fifteen times the Bureau's yearly budget for equipment.
So in late July nineteen thirty-nine, at a secret site outside Warsaw, the Poles showed French and British codebreakers everything.
They shared their Enigma copies, the sheets, the bomba and their methods.
Five weeks later, Germany invaded Poland.
They passed it on just in time.
At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman reported for work the day after Britain declared war.
Turing expected the Germans to stop typing the key twice. In May 1940, they did.
So Bletchley leaned on cribs, which were stretches of a message they could guess, like set phrases.
Such as?
One outpost in North Africa regularly sent a phrase meaning nothing special to report.
But where in the message would it be?
Slide the crib along the ciphertext, one place at a time.
Enigma never enciphers a letter as itself, so wherever a crib letter sits on the same letter, the crib can't be there.
Like here, in the second place, where an R sits on an R. That one's crossed out.
Slide on, and cross out every clash.
Of these 16 places, 9 are ruled out, without any machine at all.
The guess says what the message holds. The flaw says where it can't be.
But a crib in the right place still doesn't give you the key.
No. For that, Turing designed the bombe.
Line the crib up with the ciphertext, and each pair of letters is a link.
Draw all the links, and you get a menu. Where links close into loops, it gets powerful.
At each rotor position, the bombe guesses one letter's plug partner and follows the consequences.
And a contradiction means that position is impossible, so the drums turn on.
Gordon Welchman added the diagonal board, which uses the rule that if A is plugged to B, B is plugged to A.
Does that really make a difference?
We ran our menu through every position. Without the diagonal board, it stopped six hundred and sixty-two times.
With it, it stopped just twice, and the true stop showed E plugged to J.
The first bombe, Victory, arrived in March nineteen forty, built by Harold Keen's engineers.
By 1945 there were about 200, run by some 2,000 Wrens of the Royal Navy.
The hardest Enigma was the navy's, with three rotors from eight and stricter procedures.
Turing took it on, he said, because no one else was doing anything about it, and he could have it to himself.
It also took captured papers. In May nineteen forty-one, sailors seized codebooks and keys from U one-ten.
Through late 1941, decrypts helped steer convoys around the waiting U-boats.
Then, on the 1st of February 1942, the U-boats got a new Enigma with four rotors.
For ten months, Bletchley couldn't read them, and the wolf packs ravaged convoys.
So how did they get back in?
In October nineteen forty-two, off Port Said, sailors from H M S Petard climbed into the sinking U five-five-nine for its papers.
Two of them, Tony Fasson and Colin Grazier, were still inside when it sank, and drowned.
By December nineteen forty-two, U-boat messages were being read again.
So how much did that decide the Atlantic?
That's still argued. Radar and much else mattered too.
In the film The Imitation Game, Turing builds one machine almost alone, and calls it Christopher.
In fact, the first bombe was Victory, and breaking Enigma took thousands of people.
Thousands?
By January nineteen forty-five, Bletchley Park and its outstations had almost nine thousand staff. About three quarters were women.
And what was all that work worth?
Harry Hinsley, a veteran and later Bletchley's official historian, judged their work shortened the war by at least two years.
Others find any such number too precise. No one can run a war twice.
One of the last messages Bletchley decoded was sent from Cuxhaven, on the seventh of May, nineteen forty-five. British troops had entered the town.
And the operator signed off. Closing down forever. All the best. Goodbye.
The reflector made Enigma convenient. It also meant no letter could ever be itself.
On its own, that flaw wasn't enough.
No. But add German habits, captured papers and thousands of patient people, and it was.
Press A, and you could get any letter at all, except A.
